title: Valid Parentheses
summary: A string of ()[]{} is valid if every bracket is closed by the same type, in the right order. Return whether s is valid.
statement:
`s` contains only the characters `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`. It is valid when:

- every opening bracket is closed by a bracket of the same type,
- brackets are closed in the correct order (the most recently opened one first),
- every closing bracket has a matching opening bracket.

Return `true` if `s` is valid.
hints: The bracket that must close next is always the most recently opened one. Which data structure gives you "most recent" first?
Push opening brackets onto a stack. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener.
Return false if the stack is empty when a closer arrives, and remember to check that the stack is empty at the end.
explain: The single "(" is closed by the ")" right after it, and nothing is left open, so the answer is `true`.

title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
summary: Repeatedly delete two adjacent equal letters until none remain, and return the final string.

perf.label: a 100,000-character string
perf.gen: String h = BCB.str(50000, "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"); String a0 = h + new StringBuilder(h).reverse();

statement:
`s` has lowercase English letters. A removal deletes two adjacent, equal letters. Keep making removals until none is possible, then return the final string.

The final string is unique no matter which removals you make first.
hints: After removing a pair, the letters on both sides become neighbours and may form a new pair. Restarting the scan each time is O(n²).
Use a stack of kept letters: when the next letter equals the top, pop instead of pushing.
A StringBuilder works as the stack (append and deleteCharAt at the end), and it already holds the answer when you finish.
explain: Removing "bb" leaves "aaca", which now has "aa" next to each other. Removing that leaves "ca", which has no adjacent duplicates.

title: Backspace String Compare
summary: "#" is a backspace. Return whether s and t are equal after typing both into empty text editors.
statement:
`s` and `t` are typed into two empty text editors; `#` means backspace. Return `true` if the two editors end up showing the same text.

Backspacing in an empty editor leaves it empty.

You can simulate each editor with a stack, or walk both strings from the end and skip characters that a later `#` would delete.
constraints: `s` and `t` have lowercase letters and `#` only
hints: Building each final string with a stack (push letters, pop on #) is straightforward and O(n).
For O(1) extra space, read both strings from the end: a # means "skip one more letter to the left".
Move two pointers backwards, each skipping characters it should erase, and compare the characters that survive.
explain: In "ab#c" the "#" deletes the "b", leaving "ac". In "ad#c" it deletes the "d", also leaving "ac". The texts match, so the answer is `true`.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
summary: Evaluate an expression in Reverse Polish Notation with + - * / (division truncates toward zero) and return the result.
statement:
`tokens` is an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation: every operator comes after its two operands, as in `["2","1","+","3","*"]` for (2 + 1) × 3.

The operators are `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. Division between integers truncates toward zero. Every input is a valid expression and all intermediate values fit in a 32-bit integer. Return the value.
constraints: `tokens[i]` is an operator or an integer in [-200, 200]
hints: Numbers wait until an operator arrives. A stack holds them.
When you see an operator, pop two values, apply the operator, and push the result.
Watch the order: the first value popped is the right operand, so compute (second − first) and (second / first).
explain: Push 2 and 1, then "+" replaces them with 3. Push 3, then "*" multiplies the two 3s. This is (2 + 1) × 3, which is 9.

title: Asteroid Collision
summary: Positive asteroids move right, negative ones left, all at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller explodes (both if equal). Return the asteroids left.
statement:
`asteroids` lists asteroids in a row. The absolute value is the size; a positive sign means it moves right and a negative sign means it moves left. All move at the same speed.

When two meet, the smaller one explodes; if they are the same size, both explode. Asteroids moving in the same direction never meet. Return the asteroids that are left, in order.
hints: Only a right-moving asteroid followed by a left-moving one can collide. Keep the survivors so far on a stack.
When a left-moving asteroid arrives, it fights the right-moving asteroids on top of the stack one by one.
Pop while the top is positive and smaller; if they are equal pop once and drop the new one; if the top is bigger drop the new one. Push it only if it survives everything.
explain: The -5 moves left and meets the 10 moving right. 10 is bigger, so -5 explodes. 5 and 10 move the same way and never meet, leaving `[5,10]`.

title: Simplify Path
summary: Convert an absolute Unix-style path to its canonical form: resolve "." and "..", collapse repeated slashes, no trailing slash.
statement:
`path` is an absolute Unix-style file path (it starts with `/`). Return its canonical form, which:

- starts with a single `/`,
- separates directories with exactly one `/` and has no trailing `/` (unless it is the root `/`),
- has no `.` (current directory) or `..` (parent directory) parts; `..` at the root stays at the root.

Any other name, including `...`, is an ordinary directory name.
constraints: `path` is a valid absolute Unix path
hints: Split the path on "/" and look at the parts one at a time. Empty parts come from repeated slashes.
Keep the directories you are in on a stack: ".." pops, "." and empty parts are ignored, anything else is pushed.
Join the stack from bottom to top with "/" and add a leading "/". An empty stack means "/".
explain: The trailing slash is dropped, and there are no "." or ".." parts to resolve, so the canonical path is "/home".

title: Basic Calculator II
summary: Evaluate an expression with non-negative integers, + - * / and spaces (no parentheses). Division truncates toward zero. Don't use eval.

perf.label: an expression of about 200,000 characters
perf.gen: StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("1"); for (int i = 0; i < 50000; i++) sb.append(BCB.R.nextBoolean() ? '+' : '-').append(BCB.rnd(0, 9)).append(BCB.R.nextBoolean() ? '*' : '/').append(BCB.rnd(1, 9)); String a0 = sb.toString();

statement:
`s` is a valid expression of non-negative integers, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and spaces (no parentheses). Evaluate it with the usual precedence, where `*` and `/` bind tighter than `+` and `-`, and integer division truncates toward zero.

Do not use a built-in expression evaluator. All intermediate results fit in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: Every number fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Multiplication and division must happen before addition. Can you apply them as soon as you read the second number?
Keep a stack of terms. For + push the number, for − push its negative, and for * or / pop the last term, combine it with the number and push the result.
Apply each operator when you finish reading the number after it (or reach the end). The answer is the sum of the stack.
explain: Multiplication comes before addition, so 2*2 is 4 first, then 3 + 4 is 7.

title: Decode String
summary: Decode strings like "3[a2[c]]" where k[x] means x repeated k times; nesting is allowed.
statement:
An encoded string uses the rule `k[text]`, meaning `text` repeated exactly `k` times. Encodings can be nested, as in `3[a2[c]]` → `accaccacc`.

Decode `s` and return the result. The input is always valid, digits appear only as repeat counts, and the decoded result fits in memory.
constraints: `s` has lowercase letters, digits and square brackets
Every repeat count is between 1 and 300
hints: An inner bracket must be fully decoded before the outer one can repeat it. That nesting suggests a stack (or recursion).
On "[", save the text built so far and the repeat count, then start a fresh piece. On "]", repeat the piece and append it to the saved text.
Counts can have several digits ("10[a]"), so build the number digit by digit.
explain: "3[a]" expands to "aaa" and "2[bc]" expands to "bcbc". Joined together they give "aaabcbc".

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
summary: Return the length of the longest well-formed substring of a string made of "(" and ")".
statement:
`s` contains only `(` and `)`. Return the length of the longest substring that is a well-formed (properly matched) parentheses string.

For example in ")()())" the answer is 4, from "()()". Pieces must be contiguous, so the stray ")" in the middle of a string breaks it into separate runs.
hints: A stack of indices can tell you where the current valid run started.
Push −1 first as a base. Push the index of every "(". On ")", pop; if the stack becomes empty, push this index as the new base, otherwise the run length is i − stack.peek().
An O(1)-space alternative counts open and close brackets in a left-to-right pass and again right to left, resetting when the counts become invalid.
explain: The first "(" is never closed, but the last two characters "()" form a matched pair. The longest well-formed piece has length 2.
